label: NHSNPSA: withdrawing insulin from a pen with a syringe
title: Withdrawing insulin from an insulin pen device using an insulin syringe and needle
statement: Patient safety concerns have been identified where healthcare professionals use an insulin syringe and needle to withdraw medication directly from a patient’s insulin pen device. This practice should not happen as the strength of insulin in pen devices varies, creating a risk of overdose if the strength is not taken into consideration when determining the volume required.

plain_summary: Drawing insulin from a pen or cartridge with a syringe can cause severe hypoglycaemia or a fatal dosing error, especially with a 200 or 300 units/mL pen and a syringe marked for 100 units/mL. If an incorrect insulin dose may already have been injected, seek urgent medical advice immediately, even if the patient feels well. Otherwise, arrange a same-day review to use pen needles or another safe insulin supply, without stopping insulin abruptly.

medicine_groups.name: Insulin pen devices and pen cartridges
medicine_groups.note: Count every Australian insulin pen device and every cartridge made for a reusable insulin pen, including standard 100 units/mL and concentrated 200 or 300 units/mL products, insulin mixtures and insulin-containing combination pens. Where an ingredient or brand can identify several presentations, the supply must identify a pen device or pen cartridge. Insulin vials do not trigger this check because syringe withdrawal is intended. Exclude vials, pump-only reservoirs or cartridges, and pens that contain no insulin. Count a documented insulin pen or reusable-pen cartridge at any strength, including 300 or 500 units/mL.

rule_for_models: At any age, including when age is unknown, check every Group A supply that identifies an insulin pen or reusable-pen cartridge of any strength, excluding vials, pump-only reservoirs or cartridges, and pens that contain no insulin. For each device, use the current pharmacist answer about its withdrawal method, even if it says 'no date', when it is clear which device the answer describes. Otherwise use the most recent dated observation for that device. An answer about one device cannot settle the method for another. Ignore answers that were taken back. If anyone draws insulin from it with a syringe or plans to do so, report a finding and cite the qualifying supplies and the observation. If syringe withdrawal and plans to use it are both ruled out, report no finding for that device. If the method is missing, unknown or unresolved, cite the qualifying supplies and report a possible finding naming the missing fact "Insulin withdrawal method status".
cannot_be_seen: Supply lines and label directions do not show who gives insulin, the actual withdrawal method, the dose given, or whether an error already occurred. The pharmacist must obtain the method status. An absent answer is not a safe method.
ask_the_gp: Could the care team review the insulin administration method and dose today, and recommend pen needles or another safe insulin supply?
